episode_thesis: Katie Kaminski and Harry Moore argue that trend following proved its diversification value in Q1 2026 because it follows macro theme changes (energy and inflation up in March, equities, bonds and gold down) without forecasting them, and that its drawdowns are cyclical and self-correcting rather than evidence that it is broken. Moore's Man AHL papers add that liquid traditional markets give the best crisis Sharpe, broader alternative markets the best long-run Sharpe, and that trend's low cash need and risk-managed margin make it a strong liquid alpha for portable alpha, provided cash buffers and tail co-dependence are managed. Niels frames the evidence for a short, clean record as weak and argues the industry allocation is too small for the risks ahead.

speakers.name: Harry Moore
speakers.role: Guest; partner and senior client portfolio manager, Man AHL; co-author of the market-mix, portable-alpha and drawdown papers
speakers.speaker_note: Clean attribution. Papers discussed: A Trend Following Deep Dive (optimal market mix), Portable Alpha: Solving the Magnificent Problem, and Trend Following and Drawdowns: Is This Time Different? (June 2025, with CIO Russell).

worldview_premises.premise: Faster trend trading gives more crisis alpha; slower trading gives slightly higher Sharpe.
worldview_premises.support: Prior Man AHL work on speed.

worldview_premises.premise: Traditional markets load more on macro factors and so earn the best Sharpe in crises; alternative markets have more idiosyncratic drivers and earn a higher long-run Sharpe.
worldview_premises.support: Maximum-diversification portfolios over a market universe of about 900; principal component analysis of variance.

worldview_premises.premise: Number of markets is a poor measure of diversification: 30 stock indices are highly correlated while 30 commodities are not; regional factor versions count as separate markets.
worldview_premises.support: About 60 equity factors from roughly 15 styles times four regions; about 900 markets overall.

worldview_premises.premise: A dedicated trend mandate should be mostly trend (70-80% or more), and trend should be a divergent strategy; below that other drivers (carry, value) can show horrible left tails in a full liquidity break.
worldview_premises.support: Experience and Kaminski's divergent/convergent framing.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend is cash-efficient ($25-30 per $100 exposure) and manages to risk, so margin needs fall in a crisis; this makes it a liquid alpha that can fund margin calls for a beta index.
worldview_premises.support: Paper analysis; March 2026 example.

worldview_premises.premise: A long drawdown does not show a broken strategy; a 0.6 Sharpe, 15% volatility strategy still had a 33% drawdown lasting years, and rules that deallocate in drawdowns underperform holding.
worldview_premises.support: Simulation in the June 2025 paper.

worldview_premises.premise: Human behavioural biases explain why trend works over the long run.
worldview_premises.support: Well-documented biases literature.

worldview_premises.premise: Higher fee in macro managers is only very weakly related to higher net return, and manager indices suffer survivorship bias, so judge alpha above cheap trend and equity exposure.
worldview_premises.support: Kaminski's paper and his own hedge fund portfolio experience.

worldview_premises.premise: Alpha evaporation in active equities shifted investors to passive; portable alpha splits the decision into owning the index and finding a separate repeatable alpha, and trend on top of beta historically outperformed with more consistency than multi-strategy alpha.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The June 2025 drawdown level is captioned 'around 2022%' and read as about 22%; the SocGen Trend maximum drawdown figure is therefore uncertain.
Niels's suspicion that carry and value sleeves explain strong March results is a gut feeling without data; no manager breakdown is shown.

The statement that most trend formulations were up 3-7% YTD is a range across indices; Niels reads 7% or more for several, and the MSCI World figure was self-corrected during the recording (month -6.32% vs YTD -3.47%).
The crowding argument admits more trend capital than official AUM figures; the 2% futures-volume share is therefore a lower bound.
The market-mix findings depend on a 900-market universe including synthetic factors; execution, capacity and cost for alternative markets are not discussed.
The refutation of the 'too slow for social media' narrative rests on one recovery episode.
Portable alpha cash-buffer sizing and tail co-dependence are acknowledged as under-researched; the $40 per $100 buffer is illustrative, not derived.
Katie says equities had been down only a month and 'you got to give it some time', yet the episode concludes trend was a clear win for Q1.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs the speakers say matter: the inflation theme and oil (trend would be long oil and short bonds if it continues); whether equities, bonds and gold keep falling together; signs of a liquidity break (dash for cash) where non-trend strategies develop left tails; persistent failure of pivots in fixed income; geopolitical shocks transmitted through oil and the consumer. Horizon is weeks to months for trend and years for the allocation argument; the reason is that trend follows macro theme changes with a lag and has cyclical, self-correcting drawdowns.
reader_inferences: (reader) The three papers form one argument: trend is liquid and macro-loaded (market mix), cash-light (portable alpha), and its drawdowns are statistically normal (June 2025 paper), so it is a candidate sleeve for any diversified portfolio.

(reader) Moore's finding that traditional markets are best in a crisis and Kaminski's crisis-alpha criteria (unbiased, liquid, adaptable) reinforce each other, but both rest on stressed macro factors being the dominant driver, which the 2026 episode supported only for one month.
(reader) Niels's observation that large CTAs include carry and value sleeves, plus Moore's 70-80% trend threshold, implies the 'trend index outperformance' is partly a multi-strategy result.

(reader) Both guests treat drawdown-triggered deallocation as value-destroying, but the June 2025 paper's simulation assumes a true 0.6 Sharpe; for a strategy whose Sharpe is unknown, the rebalance advice depends on that belief.
